title: “MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?”
paragraphs:
“MY GOD, WHY HAVE YOU FORSAKEN ME?”
The Cry From the Cross That Sounds Like Despair—Until You Discover What Jesus Was Really Saying
There are words in Scripture that comfort you.
There are words that correct you.
And then there are words that stop you cold.
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
Jesus said them while hanging on a cross.
And perhaps the most unsettling thing about that sentence is not that it came from a dying man.
It came from the Son of God.
The One who said, “I and my Father are one” (John 10:30).
The One who prayed, “Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me” (John 11:41).
The One who told His disciples, “he that hath seen me hath seen the Father” (John 14:9).
Yet on Golgotha, beneath a darkened sky, with blood running from wounds made by nails, thorns, scourging, and human cruelty, Jesus cried:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
Matthew preserves the cry this way in Greek:
“Ἠλί Ἠλί, λεμὰ σαβαχθανί;”
Then Matthew gives its meaning:
“θεέ μου θεέ μου, ἱνατί με ἐγκατέλιπες;”

“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
(Matthew 27:46)
Mark records the cry as:

“Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ, λαμὰ σαβαχθανί;”
(Mark 15:34)
The Gospel writers preserve an Aramaic form of Jesus’ agonized words because this cry mattered.
But what did He mean?
Had the Father stopped loving the Son?
Had the Trinity somehow broken apart?
Had Jesus ceased to be God?
Was the Father unable to look at Jesus?
Or was something much deeper happening—something that reaches backward approximately a thousand years before the crucifixion and reaches forward all the way into your life right now?
To understand the cry of Jesus, you have to hear another cry.
“אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי”
“Eli, Eli, lamah azavtani?”
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
Those words were written in Psalm 22:1 centuries before Roman soldiers drove nails through Jesus’ hands and feet.
Jesus was crying the opening words of Psalm 22.
And once you read the rest of that psalm beside the crucifixion narratives, the darkness of Calvary begins to blaze with meaning.
Psalm 22 says:
“All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying, He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him: let him deliver him, seeing he delighted in him.”
Then stand beneath the cross in Matthew 27.
Jesus is mocked.
“He trusted in God; let him deliver him now, if he will have him.”
The resemblance is staggering.
Psalm 22 continues:
“They pierced my hands and my feet.”
Then:
“They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture.”
Now return to Golgotha.
The soldiers crucify Jesus.
Then they divide His garments and cast lots.
Jesus’ cry is therefore not floating in isolation.
It belongs to a biblical tapestry.
Psalm 22 begins with abandonment.
But it does not end there.
That changes everything.
Because toward the end of the psalm comes a declaration people sometimes miss:
“For he hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard.”
Read that again.
“He heard.”
The psalm that begins, “Why hast thou forsaken me?” moves toward vindication, worship, proclamation, and the nations turning to the LORD.
“All the ends of the world shall remember and turn unto the LORD.”
And the final generation will hear what God has done.
Psalm 22 ends:
“They shall come, and shall declare his righteousness unto a people that shall be born, that he hath done this.”
The Hebrew closing expression carries the sense that He has acted. He has done it.
And from the cross, near the completion of His suffering, Jesus cries another breathtaking word:
“Τετέλεσται.”
Tetelestai.

“It is finished.”
(John 19:30)
Not:
“I am finished.”
It is finished.
Something was accomplished at that cross.
Something sin had made necessary.
Something you and I could never accomplish for ourselves.
And this is where Calvary becomes painfully personal.
Because Jesus was not merely demonstrating what Roman crucifixion looked like.
He was giving Himself for sinners.
Isaiah had prophesied:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities... and the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Paul writes:
(2 Corinthians 5:21)
Peter writes:
(1 Peter 2:24)
Jesus Himself had said:

“For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”
(Mark 10:45)
Whatever else we say about Jesus’ cry of abandonment, we dare not empty it of the terrible reality of the atonement.
Christ truly suffered.
He truly bore sin.
He truly entered the horror of judgment.
The sinless One stood where sinners deserved to stand.
The Shepherd was struck.
The Lamb was sacrificed.
The righteous One suffered for the unrighteous.
As Peter says:

“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God.”
(1 Peter 3:18)
That last phrase may be one of the most beautiful explanations of Calvary ever written:
“That he might bring us to God.”
Jesus went there...
to bring you home.
And maybe that is where this stops being theology you can admire from a safe distance.
Because there are things you have done that nobody knows.
There are thoughts you would be terrified to have projected onto a screen.
There may be compromises hidden beneath Christian vocabulary.
Pornography deleted from a browser history.
Bitterness dressed up as discernment.
Pride disguised as spiritual maturity.
A marriage quietly collapsing.
An addiction nobody at church suspects.
A secret relationship.
Money obtained dishonestly.
Years spent pretending.
Prayers you stopped praying because somewhere inside you, you became convinced God must be tired of you.
Perhaps you know how to raise your hands during worship while your heart is breaking.
Perhaps everybody thinks you are strong.
You know better.
You know the nights.
You know the relapse.
You know the shame.
You know the thing you promised God you would never do again...
and then did again.
And shame whispers:
Hide.
The Gospel says:
Come into the light.
Shame says:
God wants nothing to do with someone like you.
The cross says:
Look at what God has done to reconcile sinners to Himself.

“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son...”
(John 3:16)
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly how seriously God takes sin.
Grace is not God looking at evil and shrugging.
Grace cost blood.
The scandal of Christianity is that the Holy One receives guilty people not because guilt is imaginary, but because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
That means repentance is not cleaning yourself up enough to deserve Jesus.
You will never deserve Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can save you.
You stop defending the darkness.
You stop renaming rebellion.
You stop negotiating with the sin destroying you.
You bring the truth into the light.
You confess.
You turn.
You trust Christ.
And grace meets you there.

“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
(Romans 3:23)
But Scripture does not stop there.

“Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”
(Romans 3:24)
Freely.
By His grace.
Through Christ.
Maybe you have spent years trying to pay a debt Jesus is calling you to bring to His cross.
Maybe you punish yourself because you think self-hatred is repentance.
It isn't.
Biblical repentance does not say, “I will hate myself until God accepts me.”
It says, “I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Jesus Christ is my only hope.”
Judas was crushed by guilt.
Peter was broken too.
Both failed Jesus terribly.
But Peter returned.
And Jesus restored him.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not because your scandal was harmless.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because failure does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Your worst chapter does not intimidate the Author of redemption.
And notice something else about Jesus' words.
Even in the agony of “Why have You forsaken Me?” Jesus still says:
“My God.”
Pain has not erased faith.
Darkness has not erased relationship.
The question itself is prayed toward God.
That matters for the person reading this who feels abandoned.
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You begged God to save the marriage.
It ended anyway.
You prayed beside the hospital bed.
The person still died.
You begged for the door to open.
It stayed closed.
You asked God why.
Then you felt guilty for asking.
But Scripture is filled with people who brought God their anguish.

“How long, O LORD?”
(Psalm 13:1)

“Why standest thou afar off, O LORD?”
(Psalm 10:1)
The Bible does not require you to pretend suffering feels beautiful.
And Jesus Himself prayed Psalm 22 from a cross.
Christian faith does not tell suffering people that pain is imaginary.
It tells them that suffering and death do not get the final word.
Because the crucified Christ did not remain in the grave.
The tomb opened.
Jesus rose.
The cry of Psalm 22 was not the final sentence of His story.
Neither were the nails.
Neither was the spear.
Neither was the stone.
“Why have You forsaken Me?” was followed by resurrection.
And resurrection changes how Christians understand every grave.
Jesus did not promise His followers a painless life.
He promised something greater.
Himself.
And because Christ is risen, those who belong to Him possess a hope suffering cannot finally kill.
Maybe you came across this article carrying something heavy.
Maybe nobody knows.
You do not need to tell strangers every detail.
But perhaps tonight is the night you stop pretending before God.
You can tell Him the truth.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that God still restores broken people.
Do not turn the comments into a performance.
Make them a place where masks come off and Christ is magnified.
And think of one person while you are reading this.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who has quietly drifted from God.
The brother who jokes about everything because he does not know how to talk about his pain.
The woman carrying shame from her past.
The Christian who thinks one more failure means Jesus is finished with them.
The unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely religion for respectable people.
Send this article to them.
There may come a night when Psalm 22 sounds less like ancient poetry and more like your own heartbeat.
On that night, come back.
Remember the beginning.
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
Then remember where the story went.
To:
“He heard.”
To:
“It is finished.”
To an empty tomb.
To a risen Christ.
To grace offered to sinners.
Grace cannot be bought. Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
If this ministry is helping you follow Jesus, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who has not opened a Bible in years.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Even invite the skeptic.
Not because Gospel Warrior can save anybody.
Jesus can.
The sky is dark.
The crowd is watching.
The religious leaders are mocking.
The soldiers are gambling for His clothing.
And the Son cries:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
Psalm 22 is unfolding before them.
Sin is being dealt with.
Prophecy is reaching fulfillment.
The Lamb is giving His life.
And soon comes the victorious declaration:
“It is finished.”
Then silence.
A tomb.
A stone.
And on the third day...
life.
That is Christianity.
Not good people climbing their way toward God.
God came near in Christ to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Not pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace entering the scandal.
Not denying the wound.
Redemption touching the wound.
Not sinners rewriting themselves.
Jesus rewriting everything.
So when shame tells you that your story is over, remember the cross.
When suffering makes heaven feel silent, remember Psalm 22.
When your past says you are permanently disqualified, remember Peter.
When sin tells you to hide, remember that Christ came for sinners.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Because the darkest cry ever heard from a cross was not the end of the story.
And if you belong to the risen Jesus...
your darkest chapter does not get to write your final sentence.
